questions.stem: The ancient theory of humours, developed by Hippocrates and later Galen, explained mental and physical illness as:
options: a conflict between the id and the superego
an imbalance of four bodily fluids
possession of the body by evil spirits
a chemical imbalance of neurotransmitters
questions.explanation: The humoral theory held that health depended on a balance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile; an excess of black bile, for example, was linked to melancholia. It was an early attempt at a natural, bodily explanation rather than a supernatural one.

questions.stem: In humoral theory, a person with a gloomy, sad temperament was thought to have an excess of which humour?
options: Black bile
Yellow bile
Phlegm
Blood
questions.explanation: Black bile was linked to the melancholic temperament; 'melancholy' comes from the Greek for black bile. Yellow bile was linked to the choleric (irritable) temperament, phlegm to the phlegmatic (calm) and blood to the sanguine (cheerful).

questions.stem: Freud's psychodynamic model explains abnormal behaviour mainly as the result of:
options: unresolved unconscious conflicts, often from early childhood
faulty learning through rewards and punishments in adulthood
an imbalance of chemicals that is inherited from parents
a society labelling unusual behaviour as a sign of illness
questions.explanation: The psychodynamic model holds that anxiety from unconscious conflicts, often rooted in childhood, can show itself as symptoms, and that defence mechanisms can become maladaptive. Learning through consequences is the behavioural explanation.

questions.stem: The medical model of abnormality treats psychological disorders as:
options: illnesses with mainly biological causes, to be diagnosed and treated
normal reactions to an unjust society that need no treatment of any kind
the result of unconscious conflicts that are uncovered in therapy
learnt behaviours that can be unlearnt through reinforcement
questions.explanation: The medical model views disorders as illnesses with biological causes, identified by symptoms, diagnosed and treated, often with medication. It can reduce blame, but critics say it underplays psychological and social factors.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest criticism of relying only on the medical model to explain depression?
options: It rejects medication completely and relies on uncovering unconscious conflicts
It can overlook life events, thinking patterns and social circumstances that contribute
It cannot use diagnosis, so it gives no way to decide who needs any treatment at all
It holds the person entirely to blame for their own symptoms, which greatly increases stigma
questions.explanation: A purely biological account can miss the contribution of stressful events, unhelpful thinking and social isolation, and so limit treatment to medication. The medical model does use diagnosis, and it tends to reduce rather than increase personal blame.

questions.stem: The biopsychosocial model, proposed by George Engel in 1977, explains mental health as:
options: the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors
the result of biological factors alone, such as genes and chemicals
the balance of four bodily fluids, which can be restored by diet
a social label that has no connection to the body or the mind
questions.explanation: Engel argued that health and illness come from the interaction of biological (genes, brain chemistry), psychological (thoughts, emotions, coping) and social (relationships, culture, income) factors, challenging a purely biomedical approach.

questions.stem: Kai has a family history of anxiety, tends to expect the worst, and recently lost his job and moved away from friends. In a biopsychosocial approach, losing his job and his friends are:
options: diathesis factors
social factors
biological factors
psychological factors
questions.explanation: Job loss and reduced social support are social factors. His family history is a biological factor and his tendency to expect the worst is a psychological factor. The model looks at how all three interact.

questions.stem: The diathesis-stress model, with roots in Paul Meehl's 1962 work on schizophrenia, proposes that a disorder develops when:
options: a person's thinking becomes negative after a single bad day
an underlying vulnerability is combined with enough stress
stress alone is enough, whatever a person's vulnerability
an inherited gene is present, whatever the environment is like
questions.explanation: A diathesis is a predisposition, often genetic or biological, that makes a person vulnerable; a disorder develops only if stressors push them past a threshold. Neither vulnerability nor stress alone is usually enough.

questions.stem: Identical twins share the same genes, yet when one twin has schizophrenia, the other often does not. How does the diathesis-stress model explain this?
options: Both may share a vulnerability, but only one met enough stress to trigger the disorder
The disorder must be entirely caused by the environment, since genes are identical
The twin without the disorder must have a completely different set of genes from the other
Schizophrenia occurs at random, so neither genes nor stress play any role in it
questions.explanation: Identical twins have a shared diathesis, but different life experiences mean one may meet stressors that push them past the threshold. The fact that concordance is high but well below 100% fits an interaction of vulnerability and stress.

questions.stem: In 'The Myth of Mental Illness' (1961), psychiatrist Thomas Szasz argued that:
options: all mental illnesses are caused by brain damage that can be seen in scans
mental illness is a myth invented by patients to avoid going to work or school
psychiatrists should have more power to detain people against their will
most so-called mental illnesses are really problems in living, not diseases
questions.explanation: Szasz argued that calling troubling behaviour an illness is a metaphor, since there is no bodily lesion, and that labels can be used to control people. He opposed involuntary treatment rather than supporting more power to detain.

questions.stem: Which is a valid criticism of Szasz's position?
options: Szasz agreed with the medical model completely, so his views add nothing new to the debate
Szasz argued that diagnosis should be used more widely, which increased overdiagnosis
Szasz claimed all people with a diagnosis should be detained, which breaches human rights
Evidence of brain and genetic factors in some disorders suggests not all are problems in living
questions.explanation: Research has found biological contributions to conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and denying illness may discourage treatment that helps. Szasz was a critic of the medical model, not a supporter, and opposed forced detention.

questions.stem: The DSM-5 is published by the ______ and the ICD-11 by the ______.
options: World Health Organization; American Psychiatric Association
Australian Psychological Society; World Health Organization
American Psychiatric Association; Australian Medical Association
American Psychiatric Association; World Health Organization
questions.explanation: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is published by the American Psychiatric Association. The International Classification of Diseases is published by the World Health Organization and covers all health conditions, not just mental disorders.

questions.stem: Why do classification systems such as the DSM-5 and ICD-11 change between editions?
options: Disorders are decided by a random vote, so the list is different every single time
Diagnoses are fixed facts of nature, so changes only ever correct the spelling mistakes
Research, social attitudes and clinical experience change how disorders are understood
Each edition must contain exactly the same number of disorders as the last edition
questions.explanation: Editions change as evidence accumulates and as social values shift; for example, homosexuality was removed as a diagnosis in 1973. This shows that what counts as a disorder is partly a social judgement, not only a biological fact.

questions.stem: A categorical diagnostic system says a person either has a disorder or does not. Why do some researchers prefer a dimensional view of normality and abnormality?
options: A continuum means that everyone who has a symptom must have a disorder
Categories are always more reliable, so they should be replaced by dimensions instead
Symptoms vary along a continuum, so a cut-off can hide meaningful differences
Dimensional systems remove the need to measure symptoms in any way at all
questions.explanation: Traits such as anxiety vary in degree across the population, so a strict yes-or-no cut-off treats people just either side of it as completely different. A dimensional approach fits the idea of a continuum from healthy to unhealthy functioning.

questions.stem: Rotter's (1966) concept of locus of control describes:
options: how far people believe outcomes depend on their own actions or outside forces
the part of the brain that controls voluntary movement and coordination
how strongly people obey the instructions given by an authority figure in charge
the number of items a person can keep in short-term memory at once
questions.explanation: People with an internal locus of control believe outcomes depend mainly on their own effort and choices; those with an external locus believe outcomes depend on luck, fate or powerful others. Rotter measured this with a questionnaire, the I-E scale.

questions.stem: After failing a driving test, Ruby says, 'The examiner had it in for me and the weather was terrible.' This statement suggests:
options: an internal locus of control
high self-efficacy for driving
a postconventional moral stage
an external locus of control
questions.explanation: Ruby attributes the outcome to factors outside her control (the examiner and the weather), which fits an external locus of control. An internal locus would explain the result by her own preparation or skill.

questions.stem: Research has linked an internal locus of control with better coping and mental health outcomes. Which is the most accurate interpretation?
options: The link is correlational, so it cannot show that an internal locus causes better outcomes
The link proves that an internal locus of control causes better mental health in every person
The link shows that an external locus causes mental illness, so it should be diagnosed
The link means that people with an internal locus can never experience distress
questions.explanation: Most locus of control research is correlational, so poor mental health could also reduce a sense of control, or a third factor could affect both. Locus of control is a belief style, not a diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which list gives the stages of change in Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical model, in order?
options: Contemplation, precontemplation, action, preparation, maintenance
Preparation, precontemplation, contemplation, maintenance, action
Precontemplation, preparation, contemplation, maintenance, action
Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance
questions.explanation: People move from not considering change (precontemplation), to thinking about it (contemplation), to planning (preparation), to making the change (action), to sustaining it (maintenance). Relapse to an earlier stage is common and expected.

questions.stem: Sam smokes and says, 'I know I should quit, and I'm thinking about it, but not yet.' Which stage of change is Sam in?
options: Contemplation
Precontemplation
Preparation
Action
questions.explanation: Sam recognises a problem and is considering change but has not committed or planned, which is contemplation. Precontemplation would mean not seeing a need to change, and preparation would involve concrete plans in the near future.

questions.stem: A counsellor finds a client is in the precontemplation stage about their drinking. According to the model, which approach is most appropriate first?
options: Focus on strategies for avoiding relapse after the drinking has stopped
End the sessions, because people in precontemplation can never change
Raise awareness of the costs of drinking without pushing for immediate action
Set a strict date for the client to stop drinking completely by the end of next week
questions.explanation: The model suggests matching help to the stage: someone in precontemplation is not yet considering change, so raising awareness and exploring the issue is more useful than action plans. Relapse-prevention strategies suit the maintenance stage.

questions.stem: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) includes validity scales. What is their purpose?
options: To make sure that every single test-taker receives a diagnosis of at least one disorder
To measure intelligence so the results can be compared with a person's IQ
To record the test-taker's heart rate while they answer each of the items
To detect test-takers who answer carelessly, defensively or to look worse than they are
questions.explanation: Validity scales check how the person approached the test, flagging random responding, faking good or exaggerating problems, so clinicians can judge how much to trust the results. The MMPI is a self-report questionnaire, not an intelligence or physiological measure.

questions.stem: In the four Ds model of abnormality, behaviour that puts the person or others at risk of harm illustrates:
options: distress
dysfunction
danger
deviance
questions.explanation: The four Ds are deviance (differing from social norms), distress (upsetting to the person), dysfunction (interfering with daily life) and danger (risk of harm to self or others). Danger is the least common of the four in people with mental disorders.

questions.stem: After a close friend dies, Ben cries often and finds it hard to concentrate for several weeks. Why would most psychologists not judge this as abnormal?
options: The distress is an expected reaction to loss, so it does not meet the idea of deviance
Ben shows no distress at all, so none of the four Ds can be said to apply to his behaviour
Grief always lasts exactly one week, so anything longer counts as a disorder
Crying is statistically rare, so his behaviour is clearly abnormal in every way
questions.explanation: Distress and some dysfunction are present, but grief after a loss is expected in context, so it is not deviant. This shows the four Ds must be applied with judgement about the situation and culture, not as a checklist.

questions.stem: A psychologist argues that using two phones at the dinner table was abnormal twenty years ago but is common today. Which approach to normality does this reflect?
options: Historical
Statistical
Medical
Functional
questions.explanation: The historical approach recognises that ideas of normal behaviour change over time. The statistical approach judges behaviour by how common it is, and the functional approach by whether it allows a person to cope with daily life.

questions.stem: In Rosenhan's 1973 study 'On being sane in insane places', eight people with no mental illness sought admission to psychiatric hospitals by reporting:
options: a long history of violent behaviour towards their own family members
a belief that they were famous people from history
being unable to sleep for several weeks before arriving
hearing a voice saying words such as 'empty', 'hollow' and 'thud'
questions.explanation: The pseudopatients reported hearing voices saying 'empty', 'hollow' and 'thud', then behaved normally once admitted. Almost all were diagnosed with schizophrenia and were later discharged with schizophrenia 'in remission'.

questions.stem: In Rosenhan's follow-up, one hospital was told pseudopatients would try to gain admission over the next three months. Staff judged 41 of 193 new patients to be impostors, although none had been sent. What does this suggest?
options: Labels have no effect on how staff perceive the behaviour of their patients
Diagnosis was strongly influenced by staff expectations, questioning its reliability
The hospital's staff had become much better at detecting real pseudopatients
Rosenhan had secretly sent 41 pseudopatients, so staff were completely accurate
questions.explanation: Staff could not reliably tell sane from insane people in either direction: first labelling sane people as ill, then labelling real patients as impostors when they expected them. This raised questions about the reliability and validity of psychiatric diagnosis at the time.

questions.stem: Which is a valid criticism of Rosenhan's study?
options: The study used too many hospitals, so the results could not be generalised to others
Rosenhan sent real patients instead of pseudopatients, so the results were invalid
Doctors may reasonably believe someone who fakes symptoms, and staff were deceived without consent
The pseudopatients were all diagnosed correctly, so the study found nothing surprising
questions.explanation: Critics argued that a doctor cannot be blamed for believing someone who lies about hearing voices, and staff were deceived without consent. More recently, a journalist's investigation questioned whether the study was reported accurately.

questions.stem: In Rosenthal and Jacobson's (1968) 'Pygmalion' study, teachers were told certain randomly chosen students would 'bloom' intellectually. Those students tended to show greater gains. How does this relate to labelling in mental health?
options: Expectations attached to a label can shape how people are treated and how they behave
Labels have no effect, because the students were chosen at random by the researchers
Intelligence is fixed, so teachers' expectations could not have changed anything
Only negative labels influence behaviour, while positive labels have no effect
questions.explanation: The Pygmalion effect shows that others' expectations can become self-fulfilling. In mental health, a diagnostic label can similarly shape how staff interpret a person's behaviour, as Rosenhan argued.

questions.stem: Films often portray people with mental illness as violent and dangerous. What does research generally show?
options: People with mental illness are never involved in violence of any kind at any time
Violence is caused by mental illness in most crimes, so the films understate the risk
Most people with mental illness are not violent and are more likely to be victims of violence
Most people with mental illness are violent, so these portrayals are accurate and fair
questions.explanation: Most people with mental illness are never violent, and people with severe mental illness are more likely to be victims than perpetrators of violence. Media portrayals linking illness and danger feed public stigma.

questions.stem: A crime podcast describes a serial offender as 'a psychopath' as if it were a formal diagnosis. Which correction is most accurate?
options: Psychopathy is a cluster of traits assessed with tools like Hare's checklist, not a DSM-5 diagnosis
Psychopathy is the most common diagnosis in the DSM-5 and can be made from news reports
Psychopathy is another name for schizophrenia, which involves hallucinations and delusions
Psychopathy is a formal diagnosis given only to people who have committed serious violent crimes
questions.explanation: Psychopathy is a set of traits, such as lack of empathy and remorse, measured with tools like the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised; the closest DSM-5 category is antisocial personality disorder. It is not the same as schizophrenia, and diagnosis from media reports is not valid.

questions.stem: R U OK? Day is an Australian campaign that mainly aims to:
options: train people to diagnose mental disorders in friends and family
replace professional treatment with conversations between friends
raise money to build new psychiatric hospitals around Australia
encourage people to check in with others and start conversations
questions.explanation: R U OK? encourages people to ask others how they are going and to listen and help them connect with support. It does not train people to diagnose, and it promotes professional help rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: Mental Health First Aid, a training program developed in Australia, teaches members of the public to:
options: diagnose disorders and prescribe medication in an emergency situation
provide long-term therapy in place of a trained psychologist
decide whether a person should be admitted to hospital
offer initial support and guide a person towards professional help
questions.explanation: Mental Health First Aid teaches people to recognise signs of mental health problems, offer initial support and encourage professional help, much as physical first aid supports someone until medical help arrives. It does not train people to diagnose or treat.

questions.stem: Men's Sheds give men a place to work on projects side by side and talk. Which factor in the biopsychosocial model do they mainly target?
options: Social connection, reducing isolation
Genetic vulnerability to disorders
Brain chemistry through medication
Unconscious conflicts from childhood
questions.explanation: Men's Sheds build social connection and a sense of purpose, which protect wellbeing; men can be less likely to seek help directly, so a shared activity offers a lower-stigma setting. Medication and genetic factors are biological.

questions.stem: Elise believes that seeking help for depression would prove she is weak, so she hides her symptoms. This is an example of:
options: public stigma
the four Ds
a diathesis
self-stigma
questions.explanation: Self-stigma occurs when a person absorbs negative public attitudes and applies them to themselves, which can stop them seeking help. Public stigma is the negative attitudes held by others in the community.

questions.stem: In the 1930s to 1950s, lobotomy was used to treat severe mental illness and its developer received a Nobel Prize in 1949. What does its later rejection show?
options: Treatments accepted in one era can later be recognised as harmful, so evidence and ethics matter
Lobotomy was proven to be the most effective treatment, so it is still widely used today
Nobel Prizes are never awarded for medical treatments, so the history must be wrong
Treatments are always rejected because they are too expensive, never because they cause harm
questions.explanation: Lobotomy caused severe and permanent harm to many people and was largely abandoned once antipsychotic medication arrived and its damage was recognised. Its history shows how context, enthusiasm and weak evidence can lead to harmful practice.

questions.stem: How does electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) as used today differ from its early use?
options: It is given while the patient is fully awake, to treat mild anxiety and everyday stress
It has been banned in every country because it has never helped any patient at all
It is used as a punishment for patients who do not follow hospital rules and routines
It is given under general anaesthetic with a muscle relaxant, mainly for severe depression
questions.explanation: Modern ECT is given under anaesthesia with muscle relaxants and consent, mainly for severe depression that has not responded to other treatments. Early ECT was given without anaesthesia and sometimes misused, which shaped its frightening public image.

questions.stem: Homosexuality was listed as a mental disorder until 1973. Today the ACT bans conversion practices that try to change a person's sexuality or gender identity. What does this history show about normality?
options: Judgements of abnormality reflect social values, which change over time
Diagnoses never change, so the 1973 decision was simply a printing error
Social values have no influence on what is classed as a disorder
Any behaviour that is uncommon must be a mental disorder
questions.explanation: Homosexuality was removed from the DSM after research and changing social attitudes showed it was not a disorder, and practices that treated it as one are now recognised as harmful. This illustrates the social construction of normality.

questions.stem: In the nineteenth century, 'hysteria', a term from the Greek word for uterus, was diagnosed far more often in women. What does this example illustrate?
options: Gender bias in a society can shape which behaviours are labelled as disordered
Women are biologically more likely than men to have every mental disorder
Diagnoses from the past were made using the same criteria as the DSM-5
The term was chosen at random and had no link to the beliefs held about gender
questions.explanation: The diagnosis reflected beliefs that women's bodies made them emotionally unstable, and it was applied to a wide range of behaviours that did not fit expectations of women. Hysteria was later dropped as a diagnosis, showing how context shapes knowledge claims.

questions.stem: Rates of ADHD diagnosis have risen in many countries. Which explanation would a psychologist need to consider before concluding that ADHD itself has become more common?
options: Diagnosis rates cannot be affected by public awareness or by access to services
ADHD did not exist before it was named, so the rise must be entirely invented
Greater awareness and changes to diagnostic criteria may have increased diagnosis
A rise in diagnosis always proves that the number of real cases has increased
questions.explanation: Diagnosis rates depend on awareness, screening, access to clinicians and how criteria are written, as well as on true prevalence. A rise in diagnoses alone cannot show whether the condition is more common or simply better recognised.

questions.stem: Scores on a stress questionnaire are normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. About what percentage of people score between 30 and 70?
questions.explanation: In a normal distribution about 68% of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two and about 99.7% within three. 30 to 70 is two standard deviations either side of 50, so about 95%.
